📌 Hidden Fees: Why “Zero Fee” Doesn’t Mean Free

Main Points
⏺ Crypto trade costs can hide in spreads, slippage, and execution routes
⏺ “No fee” often means the cost moves somewhere else
⏺ This post explains how to see the real price of an action

1️⃣ Spread — the gap between buy and sell price can already be your first hidden cost.
2️⃣ Slippage — weaker liquidity pushes your final price away from the quote.
3️⃣ Routing — an app or aggregator may choose a route that benefits it more than you.
4️⃣ Network Costs — even if the platform charges no fee, gas is still a real expense.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — compare final received amounts, check multiple routes, and don’t trust “0% fee” alone.

Final Thoughts

Trades are rarely free. If the fee isn’t visible in one line, it may live inside price, routing, or liquidity.

Here’s the breakdown on why this is a potential game-changer, especially for new pools:

The Arbitrage Engine Is Already Running

Let's talk about that brand-new pool you just saw launch. How does it earn anything on day one? The answer is simple: Arbitrage.

Europe is facing a historic birth collapse.

• EU: 3.46 million births vs 4.81 million deaths in 2025, a natural loss of 1.35 million people.

• 21 of 27 EU countries recorded more deaths than births. The EU’s population growth came entirely from migration.

• EU fertility fell to a record-low 1.34 in 2024, declining in 24 of 27 member states.

• Germany: 654,241 births in 2025, the lowest postwar total. Fertility fell to 1.32.

• France: Fertility fell to 1.56, the lowest since WWI. Deaths exceeded births for the first time since WWII.

• Italy: Just 355,000 births vs 652,000 deaths. Fertility fell to 1.14.

• Poland: 238,000 births, the lowest postwar total. Deaths exceeded births by 168,000.

• Czechia: 77,636 births, the lowest ever. Fertility fell to 1.28.

• England and Wales: Births fell 1.6% in 2025, while fertility dropped to an estimated 1.39.

• Scotland: Births reached their lowest level since records began in 1855. Fertility hit a record-low 1.25.

• Austria: Births fell to a 25-year low. Fertility hit a record-low 1.30.

• Switzerland: Fertility fell again to 1.28 in 2025.

• Greece: 68,467 births vs 126,916 deaths.

• Malta, Spain and Lithuania recorded the EU’s lowest fertility rates: 1.01, 1.10 and 1.11.

• Spain still recorded 122,167 more deaths than births in 2025, despite a small rise in births.

• Finland: Fertility rose slightly to 1.30 in 2025, but remains far below 1.87 in 2010.

Replacement level is roughly 2.1 children per woman.

Europe’s demographic crisis is no longer limited to just a few countries.

Iran Is In No Hurry to Negotiate, Trump Chalked the Delay Up To Personal Animosity 

🔤🔤🔤🔤1️⃣

Iran, in the middle of an escalating five-month war with the US, continues to stumble from one internal crisis to another – whether it is over public executions, the rising cost of living, the alleged bias of the state broadcaster or even the post-midnight destruction of pavements outside liberal-leaning Tehran cafes. 

Very little that happens in Iran, cultural or political, momentous or trivial, does so uncontested.

But there is now a growing threat of a long diplomatic deadlock, forged by mutual distrust in which neither side believes the other will stick to any agreement. 

That impasse has occurred as the war broadens, drawing in Yemen, Iraq and now Egypt. In Iran, at least, the advocates of escalation are winning. As a result, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.

Parts of the Trump administration and the Iranian opposition – including Reza Pahlavi, the son of the former deposed Shah – have never abandoned the belief that the Iranian government is on the brink of collapse.

What is true is that the picture of cohesive if brittle society presented by the millions attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei earlier this month revealed only one side of the public mood.

At a recent meeting of the supreme judicial council he argued: “Iran is engaged in a full-scale war. Today’s war is not just a war of missiles; the enemy has come to the conclusion that it cannot force the Iranian nation to surrender through military attacks. The most important battlefield today is the economy and livelihood of the people.

If economic pressures cause social discontent to form and this discontent spreads, the enormous social capital that the people have created in support of the system will be lost.”

Golshan Fathi, a Tehran human rights activist, recently wrote on her social media page: “The same sick cycle repeats (…) morning (…) the call to prayer, news of an execution (…) noon with power cuts, afternoon the water stops (…) dusk, the anxiety of war and renewed attacks on cities, and at midnight, the earth trembles.

Dissent in the form of political protest also exists, whether it is those inside jails or citizens in the squares of Isfahan protesting against the current wave of intimidatory public executions.
